disqualifying_errors: Using mass or volume as an identifying property of a substance.
Claiming flammability can be assessed without any change occurring.
Claiming a change of state produces a chemically different substance.
fixed_facts: A physical property can be measured without changing the substance's identity; a chemical property describes how it changes into a different substance.
scientific_correctness_authority.out_of_scope: Spectroscopic identification and thermodynamic property tables are beyond this course.
relationships: Physical properties include colour, state, melting and boiling point, density, hardness, and solubility; chemical properties include flammability, reactivity with acid, and resistance to corrosion.
Intensive properties do not depend on the amount of sample and can therefore identify a substance; extensive properties such as mass and volume cannot.
Observing a chemical property necessarily changes the sample, which is why chemical tests are destructive.

disqualifying_errors: Claiming repeated trials eliminate systematic error.
Discarding an outlying trial without recording that it was discarded and why.
Reporting a mean with no indication of spread or number of trials.

relationships: Repeated trials estimate random uncertainty; they do not detect or remove systematic error.

A reported result states the number of trials and the spread among them, or a reader cannot judge it.

disqualifying_errors: Claiming a larger sample of the same substance has a greater density.
Confusing density with mass, or treating a heavier object as necessarily denser.
Reporting a density with no units, or with units that are not mass over volume.
fixed_facts: Density is mass divided by volume, and it is an intensive property: it does not change with the size of the sample.
scientific_correctness_authority.out_of_scope: Thermal expansion coefficients and buoyancy calculations are beyond this course.
relationships: Density is a derived quantity, calculated from two measurements, so its uncertainty depends on both.
Because density is intensive, a small piece and a large piece of the same pure substance have the same density.
Density varies with temperature, because volume does, so a density value is quoted with the temperature it applies at.

safety_brief.h3_safety_segment_verbatim:
READ THIS BEFORE YOU TOUCH ANY MATERIAL.
HAZARD (physical): Spilled water makes floors slippery and can reach electrical outlets.
MITIGATION: Work over a tray on a low surface away from outlets, and wipe spills immediately.
HAZARD (chemical): Household substances must never be combined experimentally.
MITIGATION: This unit uses water, salt, and sugar only. Never mix cleaning products; bleach with ammonia or acid releases toxic gas. This prohibition is not disableable.
HAZARD (physical): An unknown solid chosen for the density measurement can be hazardous in itself.
MITIGATION: An adult approves every solid. Never use a battery, a magnet, a medicine, a sealed pouch, or anything carrying a printed hazard symbol.
SUPERVISION: an adult must be beside you, watching, for the whole investigation. Do not start any step until they are there.
EYE PROTECTION IS REQUIRED for this investigation. Put it on before the first step.
SAFE ORDER - do these steps in this order and do not reorder them:
  SAFE ORDER 1. Confirm no cleaning product of any kind is in the work area. If one is, stop and remove it before anything else.
  SAFE ORDER 2. Set the tray on a low surface away from every outlet, cord, and the scale's battery compartment.
  SAFE ORDER 3. Have an adult approve each solid before it is weighed; nothing with a hazard symbol, no battery, magnet, medicine, or sealed pouch.
  SAFE ORDER 4. Zero the scale, then take mass before volume, recording each trial as it is made.
  SAFE ORDER 5. Wipe every spill the moment it happens.
STOP CONDITIONS - stop at once if any of these happens:
  STOP: Stop all work if any cleaning product is brought to the work area.
  STOP: Stop if liquid approaches an outlet, cord, or the scale's battery compartment.
  STOP: Stop for any injury, burn, spill, fume, or allergic reaction and tell the supervising adult.
  STOP: Stop if a material, tool, or step is not the one this lesson specifies.
  STOP: Burn: cool it under running cool water for 20 minutes. Do not use ice, butter, or ointment.
  STOP: Splash in an eye: rinse with running water for 15 minutes, holding the eyelid open, before anything else.
  STOP: Fumes or a strong smell: leave the room, open a window from outside the room, and do not go back in to tidy up.
  STOP: Fire: do not use water. Get everyone out, close the door, and call the emergency number. Smother a very small contained flame with a metal pan lid or a fire blanket only if that is safe to do without reaching over it.
  STOP: If anyone may have swallowed a magnet, a battery, or any material from a lesson, treat it as an emergency and seek medical help at once. Do not wait for symptoms.
  STOP: A pause, break, or switch to the alternative activity is never treated as failure.
DISPOSAL: Pour salt and sugar solutions down the drain with the tap running, dry the scale and the surface, and return solids to their labelled containers. Nothing is combined with anything not on the materials list.
ALTERNATIVE (equal credit, no special equipment): Determine density from a supplied set of published mass and volume measurements, computing uncertainty by hand. Paper and calculator only.
ALWAYS - these rules hold in every lesson and nobody can switch them off:
  ALWAYS: Never mix household cleaning products; bleach combined with ammonia or acid releases toxic gas.
  ALWAYS: Never connect any investigation to mains electricity; low-voltage cells only.
  ALWAYS: Never fully seal a reacting, fermenting, oxidising, or warm mixture in any container.
  ALWAYS: Never have a flammable liquid open in the same room as a flame, hob, pilot light, heater, lamp, charger, or battery.
  ALWAYS: Never use alcohol, or any other fuel, for a flame demonstration; no open-flame demonstration is used anywhere in this package.
  ALWAYS: Never light, strike, or operate an open flame or a hob, burner, or pilot light for any investigation in this package; no lesson requires one.
  ALWAYS: Never cut, tear, puncture, or open a sealed commercial product - cold pack, hand warmer, glow stick, or smoke detector.
  ALWAYS: Never look at the sun directly or through any lens, filter, grating, or camera.
  ALWAYS: Never require a photograph, video, or voice recording as evidence of completion.
  ALWAYS: Never request or record a learner body measurement, health measurement, or medical history.
  ALWAYS: Never present invented measurements as real experimental results.

disqualifying_errors: Using mass or volume as an identifying property of a substance.
Claiming flammability can be assessed without any change occurring.
Claiming a change of state produces a chemically different substance.
fixed_facts: A physical property can be measured without changing the substance's identity; a chemical property describes how it changes into a different substance.
scientific_correctness_authority.out_of_scope: Spectroscopic identification and thermodynamic property tables are beyond this course.
relationships: Physical properties include colour, state, melting and boiling point, density, hardness, and solubility; chemical properties include flammability, reactivity with acid, and resistance to corrosion.
Intensive properties do not depend on the amount of sample and can therefore identify a substance; extensive properties such as mass and volume cannot.
Observing a chemical property necessarily changes the sample, which is why chemical tests are destructive.

safety_brief.h3_safety_segment_verbatim:
READ THIS BEFORE YOU TOUCH ANY MATERIAL.
HAZARD (physical): Spilled water makes floors slippery and can reach electrical outlets.
MITIGATION: Work over a tray on a low surface away from outlets, and wipe spills immediately.
HAZARD (chemical): Household substances must never be combined experimentally.
MITIGATION: This unit uses water, salt, and sugar only. Never mix cleaning products; bleach with ammonia or acid releases toxic gas. This prohibition is not disableable.
HAZARD (physical): An unknown solid chosen for the density measurement can be hazardous in itself.
MITIGATION: An adult approves every solid. Never use a battery, a magnet, a medicine, a sealed pouch, or anything carrying a printed hazard symbol.
SUPERVISION: an adult must be beside you, watching, for the whole investigation. Do not start any step until they are there.
EYE PROTECTION IS REQUIRED for this investigation. Put it on before the first step.
SAFE ORDER - do these steps in this order and do not reorder them:
  SAFE ORDER 1. Confirm no cleaning product of any kind is in the work area. If one is, stop and remove it before anything else.
  SAFE ORDER 2. Set the tray on a low surface away from every outlet, cord, and the scale's battery compartment.
  SAFE ORDER 3. Have an adult approve each solid before it is weighed; nothing with a hazard symbol, no battery, magnet, medicine, or sealed pouch.
  SAFE ORDER 4. Zero the scale, then take mass before volume, recording each trial as it is made.
  SAFE ORDER 5. Wipe every spill the moment it happens.
STOP CONDITIONS - stop at once if any of these happens:
  STOP: Stop all work if any cleaning product is brought to the work area.
  STOP: Stop if liquid approaches an outlet, cord, or the scale's battery compartment.
  STOP: Stop for any injury, burn, spill, fume, or allergic reaction and tell the supervising adult.
  STOP: Stop if a material, tool, or step is not the one this lesson specifies.
  STOP: Burn: cool it under running cool water for 20 minutes. Do not use ice, butter, or ointment.
  STOP: Splash in an eye: rinse with running water for 15 minutes, holding the eyelid open, before anything else.
  STOP: Fumes or a strong smell: leave the room, open a window from outside the room, and do not go back in to tidy up.
  STOP: Fire: do not use water. Get everyone out, close the door, and call the emergency number. Smother a very small contained flame with a metal pan lid or a fire blanket only if that is safe to do without reaching over it.
  STOP: If anyone may have swallowed a magnet, a battery, or any material from a lesson, treat it as an emergency and seek medical help at once. Do not wait for symptoms.
  STOP: A pause, break, or switch to the alternative activity is never treated as failure.
DISPOSAL: Pour salt and sugar solutions down the drain with the tap running, dry the scale and the surface, and return solids to their labelled containers. Nothing is combined with anything not on the materials list.
ALTERNATIVE (equal credit, no special equipment): Determine density from a supplied set of published mass and volume measurements, computing uncertainty by hand. Paper and calculator only.
ALWAYS - these rules hold in every lesson and nobody can switch them off:
  ALWAYS: Never mix household cleaning products; bleach combined with ammonia or acid releases toxic gas.
  ALWAYS: Never connect any investigation to mains electricity; low-voltage cells only.
  ALWAYS: Never fully seal a reacting, fermenting, oxidising, or warm mixture in any container.
  ALWAYS: Never have a flammable liquid open in the same room as a flame, hob, pilot light, heater, lamp, charger, or battery.
  ALWAYS: Never use alcohol, or any other fuel, for a flame demonstration; no open-flame demonstration is used anywhere in this package.
  ALWAYS: Never light, strike, or operate an open flame or a hob, burner, or pilot light for any investigation in this package; no lesson requires one.
  ALWAYS: Never cut, tear, puncture, or open a sealed commercial product - cold pack, hand warmer, glow stick, or smoke detector.
  ALWAYS: Never look at the sun directly or through any lens, filter, grating, or camera.
  ALWAYS: Never require a photograph, video, or voice recording as evidence of completion.
  ALWAYS: Never request or record a learner body measurement, health measurement, or medical history.
  ALWAYS: Never present invented measurements as real experimental results.

disqualifying_errors: Claiming repeated trials eliminate systematic error.
Discarding an outlying trial without recording that it was discarded and why.
Reporting a mean with no indication of spread or number of trials.
scientific_correctness_authority.out_of_scope: Standard deviation, confidence intervals, and outlier tests are beyond this course.
relationships: Repeated trials estimate random uncertainty; they do not detect or remove systematic error.
A systematic error shifts every trial in the same direction, so tightly agreeing results can still all be wrong.
A reported result states the number of trials and the spread among them, or a reader cannot judge it.

analysis_questions.prompt: Explain density and derived quantities in your own words and tie each claim to a specific item in your record: a measurement, a feature of your model, a documented step, or a named source. A claim with no evidence behind it is incomplete regardless of whether it is correct.

Apply density and derived quantities to a case in Matter, Measurement, and Laboratory Practice you have not worked before. Show the reasoning that produced your result, not only the result, and name the single step where that reasoning is most likely to break down.

Check your work on density and derived quantities against each stated success criterion in turn and name the one you meet least well. Revise it, then state your next step concretely enough that someone else could carry it out: what you would do, and what result would tell you it worked.

Answer the unit's essential question in two or three sentences, using density and derived quantities as your worked example and citing one piece of your own evidence: How do chemists decide what a measurement actually tells them, and how do we work safely with matter at home?

Which single piece of evidence in your record most strongly supports your conclusion about density and derived quantities? State what makes it strong — precision, repetition, independence, or directness — and name one specific change that would strengthen it further.

Name one thing your work on density and derived quantities cannot show, however carefully it was carried out, and explain what a different design or data source would have to do to answer it. State the limitation as a property of the method, not as an apology.

Audit every quantity in your record and label its origin: measured, calculated, or supplied. Every supplied quantity carries its source name, publisher, and retrieval date on the provenance line. An unlabelled quantity earns no credit, because a reader cannot tell your evidence from someone else's.

disqualifying_errors: Claiming isotopes of an element differ in proton number.
Claiming an atom's identity is set by its electron count.
Claiming the mass of an atom is distributed evenly through its volume.
fixed_facts: The number of protons in the nucleus defines the element.
Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons and different numbers of neutrons.
scientific_correctness_authority.out_of_scope: Nuclear binding energy calculations and quantum mechanical atomic models are beyond this course.
relationships: An atom has protons and neutrons in the nucleus and electrons outside it; protons are positive, electrons negative, neutrons uncharged.
Changing the neutron number gives a different isotope of the same element; changing the proton number gives a different element.
Nearly all of an atom's mass is in the nucleus, while nearly all of its volume is the region occupied by electrons.

disqualifying_errors: Claiming atomic radius increases across a period from left to right.
Claiming ionisation energy increases down a group.
Claiming atoms get larger across a period because more electrons are added.
fixed_facts: Atomic radius generally decreases across a period from left to right and increases down a group.
First ionisation energy generally increases across a period from left to right and decreases down a group.
scientific_correctness_authority.out_of_scope: Slater's rules, quantitative effective nuclear charge, and irregularities in specific trends are beyond this course.
relationships: Across a period, nuclear charge rises while electrons are added to the same energy level, so the outer electrons are pulled in more strongly.
Down a group, outer electrons occupy higher energy levels and are shielded by more inner electrons, so they are held less tightly.
The trends in radius and ionisation energy run in opposite directions because both follow from the same effective nuclear attraction.

Claiming noble gases are unreactive because they have no electrons available.
fixed_facts: Reactivity increases down group 1 and decreases down group 17.

Similar valence electron arrangements are what make the elements of a group behave similarly.

disqualifying_errors: Claiming ionic bonds form when atoms share electrons, equally or otherwise.
Claiming covalent bonds form by the transfer of electrons.
Claiming all covalent bonds share electrons equally, or that polar covalent bonds are ionic.
fixed_facts: Ionic bonding involves the transfer of electrons from one atom to another, producing oppositely charged ions held together by electrostatic attraction.
Covalent bonding involves the sharing of electron pairs between atoms.
Metallic bonding involves positive metal ions in a shared, delocalised sea of electrons.
scientific_correctness_authority.out_of_scope: Molecular orbital theory, formal electronegativity cutoffs, and band theory are beyond this course.
relationships: Ionic bonds typically form between a metal and a non-metal, where the difference in attraction for electrons is large enough for transfer.
Covalent bonds typically form between non-metals, and the sharing is equal only when the two atoms attract electrons equally; otherwise the bond is polar.
Metallic bonding leaves electrons free to move through the structure, which is what makes metals conduct and deform without shattering.

disqualifying_errors: Claiming solid ionic compounds conduct electricity.
Claiming a substance that dissolves must therefore conduct.
Claiming molecular covalent substances conduct because they contain electrons.
fixed_facts: Ionic compounds do not conduct as solids but do when molten or dissolved, because the ions become free to move.
Metals conduct in the solid state because their electrons are delocalised.
scientific_correctness_authority.out_of_scope: Conductivity measurement theory, solubility product constants, and lattice enthalpy cycles are beyond this course.
relationships: Electrical conduction requires charged particles free to move: delocalised electrons in metals, mobile ions in molten or dissolved ionic compounds.
Melting point reflects the energy needed to overcome the forces holding particles in the solid structure.
Solubility reflects whether the attractions formed with the solvent compensate for the attractions broken in the solute and the solvent.

disqualifying_errors: Claiming a polymer is a mixture of its monomers rather than a molecule built from them.
Claiming a polymer's properties depend only on which monomer it is made from.
Claiming synthetic materials are not chemically related to the natural resources they are made from.
fixed_facts: A polymer is a large molecule built from many repeating monomer units joined by covalent bonds.
scientific_correctness_authority.out_of_scope: Polymerisation kinetics, molecular weight distributions, and copolymer theory are beyond this course.
relationships: A polymer's bulk properties follow from its monomer, its chain length, its branching, and the forces between chains.
Cross-linking between chains increases rigidity and reduces the ability to melt and flow.
Materials are designed by choosing structure to obtain properties, which is why structure-property reasoning is the core of materials design.

disqualifying_errors: Claiming ionic bonds form when atoms share electrons, equally or otherwise.
Claiming covalent bonds form by the transfer of electrons.
Claiming all covalent bonds share electrons equally, or that polar covalent bonds are ionic.
fixed_facts: Ionic bonding involves the transfer of electrons from one atom to another, producing oppositely charged ions held together by electrostatic attraction.
Covalent bonding involves the sharing of electron pairs between atoms.
Metallic bonding involves positive metal ions in a shared, delocalised sea of electrons.
scientific_correctness_authority.out_of_scope: Molecular orbital theory, formal electronegativity cutoffs, and band theory are beyond this course.
relationships: Ionic bonds typically form between a metal and a non-metal, where the difference in attraction for electrons is large enough for transfer.
Covalent bonds typically form between non-metals, and the sharing is equal only when the two atoms attract electrons equally; otherwise the bond is polar.
Metallic bonding leaves electrons free to move through the structure, which is what makes metals conduct and deform without shattering.

disqualifying_errors: Claiming boiling water breaks the covalent bonds within water molecules.
Claiming hydrogen bonds are covalent bonds involving hydrogen.
Claiming non-polar molecules experience no intermolecular attraction at all.
fixed_facts: Intermolecular forces are attractions between molecules and are much weaker than the covalent bonds within a molecule.
scientific_correctness_authority.out_of_scope: Quantitative interaction energies and polarisability calculations are beyond this course.
relationships: Intermolecular attractions include dispersion forces, which act between all molecules, dipole-dipole attractions between polar molecules, and hydrogen bonding where hydrogen is bonded to nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine.
Boiling a molecular substance overcomes the forces between molecules, not the bonds within them.
Stronger intermolecular forces raise boiling point, raise viscosity, and lower vapour pressure.

hazards.description: Rubbing alcohol is flammable, its vapour is heavier than air and pools at bench level, and it is harmful if swallowed.
hazards.mitigation: STAGE A runs with no battery, charger, flame, hob, pilot light, heater, or lamp anywhere in the room. An adult dispenses no more than 30 mL per cup, caps the bottle, and removes it from the room at once. Nothing is ever tasted.

hazards.description: The poured alcohol samples - not just the bottle - are the ignition risk, and a shorting battery is an ignition source.
hazards.mitigation: STAGE A ends when every POURED SAMPLE is down the drain, the cups washed and dried, and the room ventilated ten minutes - not when the bottle is capped. Only then may a battery enter, and STAGE B runs on a different surface.

hazards.description: Passing current through salt water is electrolysis: it produces hydrogen at one lead and chlorine gas at the other.
hazards.mitigation: Each conductivity test is a touch of one to two seconds. Leads are never left standing in a solution. If bubbles form at a lead, disconnect at once, ventilate, and move to the published table.

hazards.description: Battery testing risks a short circuit that heats the leads.
hazards.mitigation: Use one 9V battery only - NEVER mains electricity, never a lithium or button cell. Keep the LED in the circuit at all times, tape the terminals before and after use, keep leads apart between tests, and let an adult make every connection.

hazards.description: Warm water can scald.
hazards.mitigation: An adult pours every warm sample and confirms with the thermometer that it reads below 50 degrees Celsius. Temperature is judged with the thermometer, never with a hand.

disqualifying_errors: Claiming solid ionic compounds conduct electricity.
Claiming a substance that dissolves must therefore conduct.
Claiming molecular covalent substances conduct because they contain electrons.
fixed_facts: Ionic compounds do not conduct as solids but do when molten or dissolved, because the ions become free to move.
Metals conduct in the solid state because their electrons are delocalised.
scientific_correctness_authority.out_of_scope: Conductivity measurement theory, solubility product constants, and lattice enthalpy cycles are beyond this course.
relationships: Electrical conduction requires charged particles free to move: delocalised electrons in metals, mobile ions in molten or dissolved ionic compounds.
Melting point reflects the energy needed to overcome the forces holding particles in the solid structure.
Solubility reflects whether the attractions formed with the solvent compensate for the attractions broken in the solute and the solvent.

Claiming inner-shell electrons participate in ordinary chemical bonding.
fixed_facts: Chemical reactions involve rearrangement of outer electrons; nuclei are unchanged.

The stability of the resulting outer-electron arrangements is part of why some rearrangements are favourable.

disqualifying_errors: Claiming oxidation is gain of electrons or reduction is loss of electrons.
Claiming oxidation can occur without a corresponding reduction.
Claiming oxidation requires the presence of oxygen.
fixed_facts: Oxidation is loss of electrons; reduction is gain of electrons.
Oxidation and reduction always occur together: electrons lost by one species are gained by another.
scientific_correctness_authority.out_of_scope: Standard electrode potentials, Nernst equation, and balancing redox in acidic or basic solution are beyond this course.
relationships: In a redox reaction, the species oxidised is the reducing agent and the species reduced is the oxidising agent.
Because electrons are conserved, the electrons lost in the oxidation equal the electrons gained in the reduction.
Combustion, corrosion, and electrochemical cells are all redox processes.

hazards.description: Vinegar is a mild acid that stings eyes and open cuts.
hazards.mitigation: Wear eye protection and gloves, cover any cut with a waterproof dressing, work over a tray, and rinse splashes with water for 15 minutes.

hazards.description: Combining household chemicals other than those listed can generate toxic gas.
hazards.mitigation: Use ONLY vinegar, baking soda, and cabbage indicator. Never add bleach, ammonia, drain cleaner, or any cleaning product. This prohibition is not disableable.

hazards.description: Warm water scalds, and household hot taps commonly deliver water above 55 degrees Celsius.
hazards.mitigation: Cabbage indicator is extracted with water an adult has poured and checked at below 50 degrees Celsius. Hot tap water is never used directly, and temperature is judged with the thermometer, never with a hand.

hazards.description: Steel wool fibres cut skin, and damp finely divided steel wool self-heats as it oxidises.

safety_brief.h3_safety_segment_verbatim:
READ THIS BEFORE YOU TOUCH ANY MATERIAL.
HAZARD (chemical): Steel wool in vinegar is an iron-and-acid reaction that slowly releases hydrogen, which is flammable in air across a wide range of concentrations.
MITIGATION: The oxidation run is NEVER put in a bag, jar, or any container with a lid. It stays in a wide open dish in a ventilated room, with no flame, hob, pilot light, heater, battery, charger, or static source anywhere near it.
HAZARD (chemical): Vinegar is a mild acid that stings eyes and open cuts.
MITIGATION: Wear eye protection and gloves, cover any cut with a waterproof dressing, work over a tray, and rinse splashes with water for 15 minutes.
HAZARD (chemical): Combining household chemicals other than those listed can generate toxic gas.
MITIGATION: Use ONLY vinegar, baking soda, and cabbage indicator. Never add bleach, ammonia, drain cleaner, or any cleaning product. This prohibition is not disableable.
HAZARD (physical): Warm water scalds, and household hot taps commonly deliver water above 55 degrees Celsius.
MITIGATION: Cabbage indicator is extracted with water an adult has poured and checked at below 50 degrees Celsius. Hot tap water is never used directly, and temperature is judged with the thermometer, never with a hand.
HAZARD (physical): Steel wool fibres cut skin, and damp finely divided steel wool self-heats as it oxidises.
MITIGATION: Wear gloves. Keep steel wool away from every battery and heat source, and never let it touch a 9V battery from an earlier unit. Warm or damp steel wool is never bagged, boxed, or binned - see the disposal steps.
SUPERVISION: an adult must be beside you, watching, for the whole investigation. Do not start any step until they are there.
EYE PROTECTION IS REQUIRED for this investigation. Put it on before the first step.
SAFE ORDER - do these steps in this order and do not reorder them:
  SAFE ORDER 1. Work in a ventilated room with no flame, hob, pilot light, heater, battery, charger, or spark source present: steel wool in vinegar releases hydrogen, which is flammable.
  SAFE ORDER 2. Put on eye protection and gloves, and cover any cut with a waterproof dressing.
  SAFE ORDER 3. An adult pours the water for the cabbage indicator and confirms with the thermometer that it reads below 50 degrees Celsius. Hot tap water is never used directly.
  SAFE ORDER 4. Make the indicator and complete the vinegar and baking-soda colour work first; that strand uses no steel wool at all.
  SAFE ORDER 5. Weigh the dry steel wool in a disposable tray on the scale - it never touches the scale surface, which stays in food use - then set it in a WIDE OPEN metal or ceramic dish. Never a bag, jar, box, or anything with a lid.
  SAFE ORDER 6. Leave the open dish undisturbed in a ventilated place away from paper, cloth, and anything that can burn, and re-weigh only once it is completely cool and dry.
STOP CONDITIONS - stop at once if any of these happens:
  STOP: Stop immediately if any cleaning product is brought near the work area.
  STOP: Stop if the steel wool or its dish feels warm: leave it open and undisturbed, ventilate the room, and wait until it is cold.
  STOP: Stop if the thermometer reads above 50 degrees Celsius.
  STOP: Never seal, bag, cap, or cover the oxidation run, and never open any inflated container near a flame, hob, or battery.
  STOP: Stop for any injury, burn, spill, fume, or allergic reaction and tell the supervising adult.
  STOP: Stop if a material, tool, or step is not the one this lesson specifies.
  STOP: Burn: cool it under running cool water for 20 minutes. Do not use ice, butter, or ointment.
  STOP: Splash in an eye: rinse with running water for 15 minutes, holding the eyelid open, before anything else.
  STOP: Fumes or a strong smell: leave the room, open a window from outside the room, and do not go back in to tidy up.
  STOP: Fire: do not use water. Get everyone out, close the door, and call the emergency number. Smother a very small contained flame with a metal pan lid or a fire blanket only if that is safe to do without reaching over it.
  STOP: If anyone may have swallowed a magnet, a battery, or any material from a lesson, treat it as an emergency and seek medical help at once. Do not wait for symptoms.
  STOP: A pause, break, or switch to the alternative activity is never treated as failure.
DISPOSAL: NOTHING FROM THIS INVESTIGATION IS EVER SEALED. Leave the steel wool spread out in its open dish, well away from anything combustible, until it is completely cold and dry - normally overnight. Then rinse it under running water until the water runs clear, squeeze it out, and put it into the OUTDOOR waste bin still wet and cold, loose, never bagged and never with paper or a battery. If the dish is warm at any point, stop, leave the room ventilated, and wait. Pour the vinegar, baking-soda, and cabbage solutions down the drain with the tap running. Bin the disposable weighing tray; it never returns to food use.
ALTERNATIVE (equal credit, no special equipment): Run the cabbage-indicator colour scale with vinegar and baking soda only - no steel wool, no hydrogen, no cool-down - and analyse published mass-change data for the rusting reaction. Kitchen materials only. This is the path to choose if the household cannot leave an open dish ventilated and undisturbed overnight.
ALWAYS - these rules hold in every lesson and nobody can switch them off:
  ALWAYS: Never mix household cleaning products; bleach combined with ammonia or acid releases toxic gas.
  ALWAYS: Never connect any investigation to mains electricity; low-voltage cells only.
  ALWAYS: Never fully seal a reacting, fermenting, oxidising, or warm mixture in any container.
  ALWAYS: Never have a flammable liquid open in the same room as a flame, hob, pilot light, heater, lamp, charger, or battery.
  ALWAYS: Never use alcohol, or any other fuel, for a flame demonstration; no open-flame demonstration is used anywhere in this package.
  ALWAYS: Never light, strike, or operate an open flame or a hob, burner, or pilot light for any investigation in this package; no lesson requires one.
  ALWAYS: Never cut, tear, puncture, or open a sealed commercial product - cold pack, hand warmer, glow stick, or smoke detector.
  ALWAYS: Never look at the sun directly or through any lens, filter, grating, or camera.
  ALWAYS: Never require a photograph, video, or voice recording as evidence of completion.
  ALWAYS: Never request or record a learner body measurement, health measurement, or medical history.
  ALWAYS: Never present invented measurements as real experimental results.

disqualifying_errors: Claiming atoms of one element are converted into another element by a chemical reaction.
Claiming nuclear particles are rearranged during ordinary chemical reactions.
Claiming inner-shell electrons participate in ordinary chemical bonding.
fixed_facts: Chemical reactions involve rearrangement of outer electrons; nuclei are unchanged.
scientific_correctness_authority.out_of_scope: Nuclear reactions belong to unit 9; orbital hybridisation is beyond this course.
relationships: In a chemical reaction, valence electrons are transferred, shared, or redistributed, and the nuclei retain their identity.
This is why elements are conserved in chemical reactions: no atom becomes an atom of a different element.
The stability of the resulting outer-electron arrangements is part of why some rearrangements are favourable.

disqualifying_errors: Claiming oxidation is gain of electrons or reduction is loss of electrons.
Claiming oxidation can occur without a corresponding reduction.
Claiming oxidation requires the presence of oxygen.
fixed_facts: Oxidation is loss of electrons; reduction is gain of electrons.
Oxidation and reduction always occur together: electrons lost by one species are gained by another.
scientific_correctness_authority.out_of_scope: Standard electrode potentials, Nernst equation, and balancing redox in acidic or basic solution are beyond this course.
relationships: In a redox reaction, the species oxidised is the reducing agent and the species reduced is the oxidising agent.
Because electrons are conserved, the electrons lost in the oxidation equal the electrons gained in the reduction.
Combustion, corrosion, and electrochemical cells are all redox processes.

analysis_questions.prompt: Produce independent mastery evidence for predicting products from periodic trends on a task you have not seen, with no worked example available. Show the reasoning, not only the result — mastery is the reasoning surviving an unfamiliar surface, and an unexplained correct answer does not evidence it.

Explain predicting products from periodic trends in your own words and tie each claim to a specific item in your record: a measurement, a feature of your model, a documented step, or a named source. A claim with no evidence behind it is incomplete regardless of whether it is correct.

Apply predicting products from periodic trends to a case in Chemical Reactions and Electron Rearrangement you have not worked before. Show the reasoning that produced your result, not only the result, and name the single step where that reasoning is most likely to break down.

Check your work on predicting products from periodic trends against each stated success criterion in turn and name the one you meet least well. Revise it, then state your next step concretely enough that someone else could carry it out: what you would do, and what result would tell you it worked.

Answer the unit's essential question in two or three sentences, using predicting products from periodic trends as your worked example and citing one piece of your own evidence: What is actually happening to electrons when one substance turns into another?

Audit every quantity in your record and label its origin: measured, calculated, or supplied. Every supplied quantity carries its source name, publisher, and retrieval date on the provenance line. An unlabelled quantity earns no credit, because a reader cannot tell your evidence from someone else's.

analysis_questions.prompt: Record two specific observations of the anchoring phenomenon for conservation of atoms and mass and one thing that does not yet fit your explanation. Turn that mismatch into a testable question: state what you would change, what you would measure, and what result would count against your own current thinking.

Explain conservation of atoms and mass in your own words and tie each claim to a specific item in your record: a measurement, a feature of your model, a documented step, or a named source. A claim with no evidence behind it is incomplete regardless of whether it is correct.

Apply conservation of atoms and mass to a case in Conservation of Mass and Quantitative Reasoning in Reactions you have not worked before. Show the reasoning that produced your result, not only the result, and name the single step where that reasoning is most likely to break down.

Check your work on conservation of atoms and mass against each stated success criterion in turn and name the one you meet least well. Revise it, then state your next step concretely enough that someone else could carry it out: what you would do, and what result would tell you it worked.

Answer the unit's essential question in two or three sentences, using conservation of atoms and mass as your worked example and citing one piece of your own evidence: If atoms are never created or destroyed, why does a reaction so often look like mass disappeared?

disqualifying_errors: Claiming mass is lost during combustion without accounting for oxygen consumed and gases released.
Claiming atoms are created or destroyed in a chemical reaction.
Concluding that mass is not conserved from an open-container measurement.
fixed_facts: The number of atoms of each element is identical before and after a chemical reaction, so mass is conserved.
scientific_correctness_authority.out_of_scope: Mass-energy equivalence, which does apply to nuclear reactions, is unit 9 work.
relationships: Atoms are neither created nor destroyed in chemical reactions; they are rearranged among substances.
Conservation of atoms is the reason chemical equations must balance and the reason mass calculations work.
An apparent mass change in an open system means matter crossed the system boundary, most often as a gas.

disqualifying_errors: Claiming mass is lost during combustion without accounting for oxygen consumed and gases released.
Claiming atoms are created or destroyed in a chemical reaction.
Concluding that mass is not conserved from an open-container measurement.
fixed_facts: The number of atoms of each element is identical before and after a chemical reaction, so mass is conserved.
scientific_correctness_authority.out_of_scope: Mass-energy equivalence, which does apply to nuclear reactions, is unit 9 work.
relationships: Atoms are neither created nor destroyed in chemical reactions; they are rearranged among substances.
Conservation of atoms is the reason chemical equations must balance and the reason mass calculations work.
An apparent mass change in an open system means matter crossed the system boundary, most often as a gas.

disqualifying_errors: Altering a subscript in a chemical formula in order to balance an equation.
Presenting an equation as balanced when the atom counts differ between sides.
Claiming coefficients represent masses rather than numbers of particles or moles.
fixed_facts: Balancing an equation is done by changing coefficients only; subscripts in a formula are never changed to make an equation balance.
scientific_correctness_authority.out_of_scope: Balancing redox half-reactions in solution and matrix methods are beyond this course.
relationships: A balanced equation has the same number of atoms of each element on both sides, and the same total charge.
Coefficients represent relative numbers of particles or moles, and they scale the whole formula unit they precede.
Changing a subscript changes the substance, which is why balancing never alters subscripts.

disqualifying_errors: Computing an energy change from bond breaking alone, ignoring bond formation.
Reversing the sign convention so that bond breaking is treated as releasing energy.

scientific_correctness_authority.out_of_scope: Hess's law cycles and calorimetric enthalpy determination are acceptable but not required.
relationships: The net energy change is the total energy needed to break all bonds in the reactants minus the total released in forming all bonds in the products.
If more energy is released in forming bonds than was required to break them, the reaction is exothermic; otherwise it is endothermic.
Bond energy values are averages across compounds, so calculations from them give estimates rather than exact results.

disqualifying_errors: Claiming a device can be one hundred per cent efficient in converting energy to useful work.
Claiming the second law is violated by any local decrease in disorder, without accounting for the surroundings.
Confusing conservation of energy with conservation of useful energy.
fixed_facts: Energy spontaneously disperses; concentrating it in a system requires energy input from elsewhere.
scientific_correctness_authority.out_of_scope: Quantitative entropy calculation and statistical thermodynamics are beyond this course.
relationships: Energy is conserved in every process, but its usefulness decreases as it disperses into the surroundings.
A refrigerator or heat pump moves thermal energy from cooler to warmer only because work is done on it, so the overall dispersal still increases.
This is why no device converts all energy input into useful output, and why perpetual motion machines are impossible.

safety_brief.h3_safety_segment_verbatim:
READ THIS BEFORE YOU TOUCH ANY MATERIAL.
HAZARD (chemical): A cold pack holds a salt that irritates skin and eyes and is harmful if swallowed; a torn hand warmer releases self-heating iron powder reaching about 65 degrees Celsius, an inhalation and ignition hazard.
MITIGATION: OBSERVED FROM THE OUTSIDE ONLY: never cut, torn, punctured, or opened, and the contents never touched or tasted. If one leaks, an adult bags and bins it and contact is rinsed 15 minutes. Not disableable.
HAZARD (chemical): Calcium chloride releases substantial heat when dissolving and can burn skin and eyes, and pouring water onto the solid spatters hot solution.
MITIGATION: OPTIONAL. An adult handles the solid from its original labelled container - never bulk road salt. Eye protection and gloves; under one teaspoon; SOLID IS ALWAYS ADDED TO THE WATER, never the reverse; never touched warm.
HAZARD (chemical): Ice-melt calcium chloride is not a food grade and leaves residue on whatever holds, stirs, or measures it.
MITIGATION: The calcium chloride route runs in disposable cups with a disposable stirrer, binned after one use. No mug, tumbler, flask, bottle, or drinking cup holds it, and nothing that touches it returns to food or drinking use.
HAZARD (physical): Solutions can become hot enough to burn.
MITIGATION: Use an insulated cup on a tray, stir with the thermometer rather than a finger, judge temperature only from the thermometer, and stop if the solution exceeds 50 degrees Celsius.
SUPERVISION: an adult must be beside you, watching, for the whole investigation. Do not start any step until they are there.
EYE PROTECTION IS REQUIRED for this investigation. Put it on before the first step.
SAFE ORDER - do these steps in this order and do not reorder them:
  SAFE ORDER 1. Read the phenomenon with the commercial cold pack and hand warmer SEALED. They are squeezed and felt through the pouch only, and are never cut, torn, punctured, or opened.
  SAFE ORDER 2. Put on eye protection; if the calcium chloride route runs, put on gloves too and let the adult handle the solid from its original labelled container.
  SAFE ORDER 3. If the calcium chloride route runs, set out its DISPOSABLE cups and stirrer now. Calcium chloride is never put in a mug, tumbler, flask, bottle, or drinking cup, and nothing that touches it returns to food or drinking use.
  SAFE ORDER 4. Set the insulated cup on a tray and record the starting temperature before anything is added.
  SAFE ORDER 5. ALWAYS ADD THE SOLID TO THE WATER, a little at a time, never water to the solid. Keep every quantity under one teaspoon.
  SAFE ORDER 6. Stir with the thermometer, not a finger, and read temperature only from the thermometer.
  SAFE ORDER 7. Stop at 50 degrees Celsius and let the solution stand untouched until it is cool.
STOP CONDITIONS - stop at once if any of these happens:
  STOP: Stop if anyone cuts, tears, punctures, or opens a commercial cold pack or hand warmer.
  STOP: Stop if the thermometer reads above 50 degrees Celsius.
  STOP: Stop if calcium chloride contacts skin and rinse thoroughly for 15 minutes.
  STOP: Skip the calcium chloride route entirely if eye protection and gloves are not available.
  STOP: Stop for any injury, burn, spill, fume, or allergic reaction and tell the supervising adult.
  STOP: Stop if a material, tool, or step is not the one this lesson specifies.
  STOP: Burn: cool it under running cool water for 20 minutes. Do not use ice, butter, or ointment.
  STOP: Splash in an eye: rinse with running water for 15 minutes, holding the eyelid open, before anything else.
  STOP: Fumes or a strong smell: leave the room, open a window from outside the room, and do not go back in to tidy up.
  STOP: Fire: do not use water. Get everyone out, close the door, and call the emergency number. Smother a very small contained flame with a metal pan lid or a fire blanket only if that is safe to do without reaching over it.
  STOP: If anyone may have swallowed a magnet, a battery, or any material from a lesson, treat it as an emergency and seek medical help at once. Do not wait for symptoms.
  STOP: A pause, break, or switch to the alternative activity is never treated as failure.
DISPOSAL: Let every solution cool to room temperature in its OPEN cup before it is moved; never cap or store a warm solution. Pour cooled Epsom-salt, baking-soda, and vinegar solutions down the drain with the tap running. Dilute a cooled calcium chloride solution with plenty of cold water as it goes down the drain, then bin the disposable cups and stirrer that held it; they never return to food or drinking use. The cold pack and the hand warmer go into the household bin STILL SEALED - never opened, drained, or cut.
ALTERNATIVE (equal credit, no special equipment): Use Epsom salt and baking soda with vinegar only - both mild - to observe cooling and mild warming, or work entirely from a published table of dissolution enthalpies and bond energies. Kitchen materials or paper.
ALWAYS - these rules hold in every lesson and nobody can switch them off:
  ALWAYS: Never mix household cleaning products; bleach combined with ammonia or acid releases toxic gas.
  ALWAYS: Never connect any investigation to mains electricity; low-voltage cells only.
  ALWAYS: Never fully seal a reacting, fermenting, oxidising, or warm mixture in any container.
  ALWAYS: Never have a flammable liquid open in the same room as a flame, hob, pilot light, heater, lamp, charger, or battery.
  ALWAYS: Never use alcohol, or any other fuel, for a flame demonstration; no open-flame demonstration is used anywhere in this package.
  ALWAYS: Never light, strike, or operate an open flame or a hob, burner, or pilot light for any investigation in this package; no lesson requires one.
  ALWAYS: Never cut, tear, puncture, or open a sealed commercial product - cold pack, hand warmer, glow stick, or smoke detector.
  ALWAYS: Never look at the sun directly or through any lens, filter, grating, or camera.
  ALWAYS: Never require a photograph, video, or voice recording as evidence of completion.
  ALWAYS: Never request or record a learner body measurement, health measurement, or medical history.
  ALWAYS: Never present invented measurements as real experimental results.

disqualifying_errors: Computing an energy change from bond breaking alone, ignoring bond formation.
Reversing the sign convention so that bond breaking is treated as releasing energy.

scientific_correctness_authority.out_of_scope: Hess's law cycles and calorimetric enthalpy determination are acceptable but not required.
relationships: The net energy change is the total energy needed to break all bonds in the reactants minus the total released in forming all bonds in the products.

Bond energy values are averages across compounds, so calculations from them give estimates rather than exact results.

fixed_facts: Thermal energy transfers spontaneously from the higher-temperature body to the lower-temperature one until they reach the same temperature.

relationships: Two bodies in thermal contact exchange energy until their temperatures are equal, which is thermal equilibrium.

The energy lost by one body equals the energy gained by the other and its surroundings; energy is conserved.

disqualifying_errors: Claiming a catalyst is consumed by the reaction it catalyses.
Claiming a catalyst increases the yield or shifts the equilibrium position.
Claiming a catalyst supplies the activation energy rather than lowering it.
fixed_facts: A catalyst increases reaction rate by providing a pathway with lower activation energy, and it is not consumed by the reaction.
scientific_correctness_authority.out_of_scope: Catalytic mechanisms, turnover number, and heterogeneous catalysis theory are beyond this course.
relationships: A catalyst lowers the activation energy, so a larger fraction of collisions is effective at any given temperature.
A catalyst does not change the overall energy change of the reaction or the position of equilibrium; it speeds the forward and reverse directions equally.
Enzymes are biological catalysts and follow the same principles.

  SAFE ORDER 3. Put on eye protection and set every cup on a tray.

safety_brief.h3_safety_segment_verbatim:
READ THIS BEFORE YOU TOUCH ANY MATERIAL.
HAZARD (chemical): A glow stick holds an internal glass ampoule, irritant esters, and hydrogen peroxide.
MITIGATION: Bend to activate; never cut, bite, open, or mouth a glow stick. If one splits, nobody touches it: rinse any contact 15 minutes and an adult bags and bins it. This prohibition is not disableable.
HAZARD (chemical): Vinegar and effervescent tablets irritate eyes.
MITIGATION: Wear eye protection, work over a tray, and rinse splashes with water.
HAZARD (physical): Warm water can scald and glass can break with thermal shock.
MITIGATION: An adult pours every warm sample and confirms with the thermometer that it reads below 50 degrees Celsius. Use plastic or unbreakable cups only.
SUPERVISION: an adult must be beside you, watching, for the whole investigation. Do not start any step until they are there.
EYE PROTECTION IS REQUIRED for this investigation. Put it on before the first step.
SAFE ORDER - do these steps in this order and do not reorder them:
  SAFE ORDER 1. Bend the glow stick to activate it; never cut, bite, or open one, and never put one in a mouth.
  SAFE ORDER 2. An adult prepares the warm water and confirms with the thermometer that it reads below 50 degrees Celsius before any cup is placed.
  SAFE ORDER 3. Put on eye protection and set every cup on a tray.
  SAFE ORDER 4. Run one condition at a time, from cold to warm, recording each timing before anything is changed.
  SAFE ORDER 5. Never cap, seal, or cover a cup while it is fizzing.
STOP CONDITIONS - stop at once if any of these happens:
  STOP: Stop if the thermometer reads above 50 degrees Celsius. Water temperature is judged with the thermometer, never with a hand.
  STOP: Stop if a glow stick splits or leaks, and let an adult bag and bin it.
  STOP: Never seal, cap, or cover a container during an effervescent reaction.
  STOP: Stop for any injury, burn, spill, fume, or allergic reaction and tell the supervising adult.
  STOP: Stop if a material, tool, or step is not the one this lesson specifies.
  STOP: Burn: cool it under running cool water for 20 minutes. Do not use ice, butter, or ointment.
  STOP: Splash in an eye: rinse with running water for 15 minutes, holding the eyelid open, before anything else.
  STOP: Fumes or a strong smell: leave the room, open a window from outside the room, and do not go back in to tidy up.
  STOP: Fire: do not use water. Get everyone out, close the door, and call the emergency number. Smother a very small contained flame with a metal pan lid or a fire blanket only if that is safe to do without reaching over it.
  STOP: If anyone may have swallowed a magnet, a battery, or any material from a lesson, treat it as an emergency and seek medical help at once. Do not wait for symptoms.
  STOP: A pause, break, or switch to the alternative activity is never treated as failure.
DISPOSAL: Pour all vinegar and effervescent solutions down the drain with the tap running, rinse and dry the cups, and wipe the tray. A cup is never sealed, capped, or covered while it is still fizzing. A spent glow stick goes into the household bin intact. If one has split or leaked, nobody touches it: an adult bags it and bins it and any contact is rinsed for 15 minutes.
ALTERNATIVE (equal credit, no special equipment): Vary only surface area and concentration at room temperature - whole versus crushed tablet, full-strength versus diluted vinegar - eliminating all heating. Or analyse a published rate-versus-temperature dataset. Kitchen materials or paper.

  ALWAYS: Never mix household cleaning products; bleach combined with ammonia or acid releases toxic gas.
  ALWAYS: Never connect any investigation to mains electricity; low-voltage cells only.
  ALWAYS: Never fully seal a reacting, fermenting, oxidising, or warm mixture in any container.
  ALWAYS: Never have a flammable liquid open in the same room as a flame, hob, pilot light, heater, lamp, charger, or battery.
  ALWAYS: Never use alcohol, or any other fuel, for a flame demonstration; no open-flame demonstration is used anywhere in this package.
  ALWAYS: Never light, strike, or operate an open flame or a hob, burner, or pilot light for any investigation in this package; no lesson requires one.

  ALWAYS: Never require a photograph, video, or voice recording as evidence of completion.
  ALWAYS: Never request or record a learner body measurement, health measurement, or medical history.
  ALWAYS: Never present invented measurements as real experimental results.

disqualifying_errors: Claiming a catalyst is consumed by the reaction it catalyses.
Claiming a catalyst increases the yield or shifts the equilibrium position.
Claiming a catalyst supplies the activation energy rather than lowering it.
fixed_facts: A catalyst increases reaction rate by providing a pathway with lower activation energy, and it is not consumed by the reaction.
scientific_correctness_authority.out_of_scope: Catalytic mechanisms, turnover number, and heterogeneous catalysis theory are beyond this course.
relationships: A catalyst lowers the activation energy, so a larger fraction of collisions is effective at any given temperature.
A catalyst does not change the overall energy change of the reaction or the position of equilibrium; it speeds the forward and reverse directions equally.
Enzymes are biological catalysts and follow the same principles.

safety_brief.h3_safety_segment_verbatim:
READ THIS BEFORE YOU TOUCH ANY MATERIAL.
HAZARD (chemical): Acidic and basic solutions sting eyes and irritate skin.
MITIGATION: Wear eye protection, work over a tray, use small volumes with droppers, and rinse any splash with water for 15 minutes.
HAZARD (chemical): Household chemical mixing beyond the listed materials can produce toxic gas.
MITIGATION: Use ONLY cabbage indicator, vinegar, baking soda, and carbonated water. Never introduce a cleaning product. This prohibition is not disableable.
HAZARD (physical): A sealed carbonated bottle is a pressure vessel, and warming or shaking it turns the cap into a projectile.
MITIGATION: A carbonated bottle is never warmed above 40 degrees Celsius, never shaken while closed, and is always opened slowly with the cap pointed away from every face.
HAZARD (physical): Warm water can scald.
MITIGATION: An adult pours the warm bath and confirms with the thermometer that it reads below 50 degrees Celsius. Temperature is judged with the thermometer, never with a hand.
SUPERVISION: an adult must be beside you, watching, for the whole investigation. Do not start any step until they are there.
EYE PROTECTION IS REQUIRED for this investigation. Put it on before the first step.
SAFE ORDER - do these steps in this order and do not reorder them:
  SAFE ORDER 1. Confirm no cleaning product is in the work area; only cabbage indicator, vinegar, baking soda, and carbonated water are used.
  SAFE ORDER 2. Put on eye protection and set the droppers and cups on a tray.
  SAFE ORDER 3. An adult prepares the baths and confirms with the thermometer that the warm bath reads below 50 degrees Celsius, and that any closed carbonated bottle stays below 40.
  SAFE ORDER 4. Change one condition at a time and record the colour before making the next change.
  SAFE ORDER 5. Never shake a closed carbonated bottle; open it slowly, with the cap pointed away from every face.
STOP CONDITIONS - stop at once if any of these happens:
  STOP: Stop if any solution contacts the eyes and rinse for 15 minutes.
  STOP: Stop if the thermometer reads above 50 degrees Celsius, or above 40 degrees Celsius for any closed carbonated bottle.
  STOP: Stop all work if a cleaning product enters the work area.
  STOP: Stop for any injury, burn, spill, fume, or allergic reaction and tell the supervising adult.
  STOP: Stop if a material, tool, or step is not the one this lesson specifies.
  STOP: Burn: cool it under running cool water for 20 minutes. Do not use ice, butter, or ointment.
  STOP: Splash in an eye: rinse with running water for 15 minutes, holding the eyelid open, before anything else.
  STOP: Fumes or a strong smell: leave the room, open a window from outside the room, and do not go back in to tidy up.
  STOP: Fire: do not use water. Get everyone out, close the door, and call the emergency number. Smother a very small contained flame with a metal pan lid or a fire blanket only if that is safe to do without reaching over it.
  STOP: If anyone may have swallowed a magnet, a battery, or any material from a lesson, treat it as an emergency and seek medical help at once. Do not wait for symptoms.
  STOP: A pause, break, or switch to the alternative activity is never treated as failure.
DISPOSAL: Pour all indicator, vinegar, baking-soda, and carbonated solutions down the drain with the tap running, rinse the cups and droppers, and wipe the tray. Open and empty any carbonated bottle before recycling it. No solution is stored or reused.
ALTERNATIVE (equal credit, no special equipment): Observe the carbon-dioxide equilibrium in carbonated water alone - sealed versus open, cool versus warm - with no indicator chemistry, or reason from a published equilibrium dataset. Kitchen materials or paper.
ALWAYS - these rules hold in every lesson and nobody can switch them off:
  ALWAYS: Never mix household cleaning products; bleach combined with ammonia or acid releases toxic gas.
  ALWAYS: Never connect any investigation to mains electricity; low-voltage cells only.
  ALWAYS: Never fully seal a reacting, fermenting, oxidising, or warm mixture in any container.
  ALWAYS: Never have a flammable liquid open in the same room as a flame, hob, pilot light, heater, lamp, charger, or battery.
  ALWAYS: Never use alcohol, or any other fuel, for a flame demonstration; no open-flame demonstration is used anywhere in this package.
  ALWAYS: Never light, strike, or operate an open flame or a hob, burner, or pilot light for any investigation in this package; no lesson requires one.
  ALWAYS: Never cut, tear, puncture, or open a sealed commercial product - cold pack, hand warmer, glow stick, or smoke detector.
  ALWAYS: Never look at the sun directly or through any lens, filter, grating, or camera.
  ALWAYS: Never require a photograph, video, or voice recording as evidence of completion.
  ALWAYS: Never request or record a learner body measurement, health measurement, or medical history.
  ALWAYS: Never present invented measurements as real experimental results.

disqualifying_errors: Claiming the system returns exactly to its original conditions after a disturbance.
Claiming a catalyst shifts the position of equilibrium.
Claiming adding an inert gas at constant volume shifts a gas-phase equilibrium.
fixed_facts: A system at equilibrium responds to a change in conditions by shifting in the direction that partially counteracts that change.
scientific_correctness_authority.out_of_scope: Quantitative prediction of the new equilibrium position is beyond this course.
relationships: Changing concentration, pressure, or temperature disturbs the balance of forward and reverse rates, and the system shifts until they are equal again.
The shift partially offsets the change; it does not restore the original conditions.
Temperature is the only one of these changes that alters the equilibrium position by changing the balance of the reaction's own energetics rather than by changing amounts.

disqualifying_errors: Claiming half-life can be changed by heating, cooling, or chemically combining the substance.
Claiming a sample is completely gone after two half-lives.
Claiming radioactive decay is a chemical reaction involving electrons.
fixed_facts: Half-life is the time for half of the nuclei in a sample to decay, and it is unaffected by temperature, pressure, or chemical combination.
Alpha decay reduces the atomic number by two and the mass number by four; beta-minus decay increases the atomic number by one and leaves the mass number unchanged.
scientific_correctness_authority.out_of_scope: Decay constants, activity units, and dosimetry are beyond this course.
relationships: Radioactive decay is a nuclear process, so it changes the element, unlike chemical reactions.
Decay of an individual nucleus is random, while the behaviour of a large sample follows a predictable exponential pattern.
Half-life is a constant for a given nuclide and does not depend on how much of the sample remains.

disqualifying_errors: Claiming mass is conserved exactly in nuclear reactions in the same way it is in chemical ones.
Claiming chemical and nuclear energy releases are of comparable magnitude per reaction.
Claiming nuclear energy comes from breaking bonds between atoms.
fixed_facts: In nuclear reactions a small amount of mass is converted to energy, following the mass-energy relationship, which is why nuclear energy release is millions of times larger per event than chemical energy release.
scientific_correctness_authority.out_of_scope: Relativistic mechanics and binding energy computation are beyond this course.
relationships: The energy released in a nuclear reaction corresponds to the mass difference between the initial and final nuclei.
Chemical reactions rearrange electrons and involve mass changes far too small to measure; nuclear reactions do not.
This difference in scale is why a small mass of nuclear fuel yields energy comparable to a very large mass of chemical fuel.

safety_brief.h3_safety_segment_verbatim:
READ THIS BEFORE YOU TOUCH ANY MATERIAL.
HAZARD (physical): A domestic smoke detector contains a sealed radioactive source and is safe only while it stays intact.
MITIGATION: A smoke detector is never opened, dismantled, or taken apart, and its source is never removed or handled. A working smoke alarm is a safety device and stays installed and intact. This prohibition is not disableable.
HAZARD (physical): Large numbers of small counters spread and can be a choking hazard.
MITIGATION: Work in a shallow tray, keep counters away from young children, and count them back at the end.
HAZARD (emotional): Nuclear topics can raise anxiety about weapons or accidents.
MITIGATION: Content stays on decay physics, energy scale, and engineering trade-offs; the learner may pause or redirect to the materials strand at any point.
SUPERVISION: you may work on this independently. Tell an adult before you start anyway.
SAFE ORDER - do these steps in this order and do not reorder them:
  SAFE ORDER 1. Set the shallow tray down and move young children out of the work area before counters come out.
  SAFE ORDER 2. Count the 100 counters in and record the starting number.
  SAFE ORDER 3. Run each generation, removing and recording before the next throw.
  SAFE ORDER 4. Never open, dismantle, or take apart a smoke detector; it is discussed as a phenomenon and never handled as equipment.
  SAFE ORDER 5. Count every counter back in and confirm the total before leaving.
STOP CONDITIONS - stop at once if any of these happens:
  STOP: Pause if nuclear content becomes distressing and continue with the materials trade-off strand.
  STOP: Stop if anyone begins to open or dismantle a smoke detector.
  STOP: NO RADIOACTIVE SOURCE OF ANY KIND IS USED OR ACQUIRED IN THIS UNIT.
  STOP: Stop for any injury, burn, spill, fume, or allergic reaction and tell the supervising adult.
  STOP: Stop if a material, tool, or step is not the one this lesson specifies.
  STOP: Burn: cool it under running cool water for 20 minutes. Do not use ice, butter, or ointment.
  STOP: Splash in an eye: rinse with running water for 15 minutes, holding the eyelid open, before anything else.
  STOP: Fumes or a strong smell: leave the room, open a window from outside the room, and do not go back in to tidy up.
  STOP: Fire: do not use water. Get everyone out, close the door, and call the emergency number. Smother a very small contained flame with a metal pan lid or a fire blanket only if that is safe to do without reaching over it.
  STOP: If anyone may have swallowed a magnet, a battery, or any material from a lesson, treat it as an emergency and seek medical help at once. Do not wait for symptoms.
  STOP: A pause, break, or switch to the alternative activity is never treated as failure.
DISPOSAL: Counters go back into a labelled container stored out of reach of young children. No radioactive source is used or acquired at any point and no smoke detector is opened, so there is nothing hazardous to dispose of.
ALTERNATIVE (equal credit, no special equipment): Model half-life with a single die and tally marks on paper instead of 100 coins, then complete the trade-off analysis from published materials data. Paper only.
ALWAYS - these rules hold in every lesson and nobody can switch them off:
  ALWAYS: Never mix household cleaning products; bleach combined with ammonia or acid releases toxic gas.
  ALWAYS: Never connect any investigation to mains electricity; low-voltage cells only.
  ALWAYS: Never fully seal a reacting, fermenting, oxidising, or warm mixture in any container.
  ALWAYS: Never have a flammable liquid open in the same room as a flame, hob, pilot light, heater, lamp, charger, or battery.
  ALWAYS: Never use alcohol, or any other fuel, for a flame demonstration; no open-flame demonstration is used anywhere in this package.
  ALWAYS: Never light, strike, or operate an open flame or a hob, burner, or pilot light for any investigation in this package; no lesson requires one.
  ALWAYS: Never cut, tear, puncture, or open a sealed commercial product - cold pack, hand warmer, glow stick, or smoke detector.
  ALWAYS: Never look at the sun directly or through any lens, filter, grating, or camera.
  ALWAYS: Never require a photograph, video, or voice recording as evidence of completion.
  ALWAYS: Never request or record a learner body measurement, health measurement, or medical history.
  ALWAYS: Never present invented measurements as real experimental results.

disqualifying_errors: Claiming isotopes of an element differ chemically in a substantial way.
Claiming the mass number is the mass in grams.
Claiming an element's isotopes have different proton numbers.
fixed_facts: The atomic number is the number of protons and identifies the element; the mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons.
scientific_correctness_authority.out_of_scope: Nuclear shell models and binding energy per nucleon curves are acceptable to reference but not required.
relationships: Isotopes of an element share the proton number and differ in neutron number, and therefore in mass number.
Isotopes of an element have essentially identical chemical behaviour, because chemistry depends on electrons, while their nuclear stability can differ greatly.
The mass listed on the periodic table is a weighted average over an element's naturally occurring isotopes.

disqualifying_errors: Claiming half-life can be changed by heating, cooling, or chemically combining the substance.
Claiming a sample is completely gone after two half-lives.
Claiming radioactive decay is a chemical reaction involving electrons.
fixed_facts: Half-life is the time for half of the nuclei in a sample to decay, and it is unaffected by temperature, pressure, or chemical combination.
Alpha decay reduces the atomic number by two and the mass number by four; beta-minus decay increases the atomic number by one and leaves the mass number unchanged.
scientific_correctness_authority.out_of_scope: Decay constants, activity units, and dosimetry are beyond this course.
relationships: Radioactive decay is a nuclear process, so it changes the element, unlike chemical reactions.
Decay of an individual nucleus is random, while the behaviour of a large sample follows a predictable exponential pattern.
Half-life is a constant for a given nuclide and does not depend on how much of the sample remains.

instruction:
Focus for today: fission, inside the unit The Nucleus, Nuclear Energy, and a Chemistry Engineering Capstone.
Anchoring phenomenon: A smoke detector contains a radioactive source, runs for a decade, and is safe to hold - while a comparable mass of the same isotope in another form would not be. SAFETY: the smoke detector in this unit is observed sealed and from the outside only - never cut, torn, punctured, bitten, dismantled, or opened, and the contents are never touched or tasted.
Unit question: What changes when the nucleus itself is rearranged, and how should a society weigh the trade-offs?
What you are aiming at: Produce performance-task evidence for fission that a reader could check independently. Explain fission using evidence, a model, or a documented process rather than an unsupported answer. Apply fission to a task the learner has not seen before, showing the reasoning that produced the result. Check and revise the work on fission against the stated success criteria and name the next step.
You have met the target when: The learner completes the central task about fission. The learner supplies evidence, reasoning, a model, or a documented process, not a bare answer. The learner checks or revises the work and identifies one specific next step. Any quantity the learner reports is one the learner measured, computed, or cited to a named published source.
The work itself: SAFETY FIRST - SUPERVISION: you may work on this independently. Tell an adult before you start anyway. Read the safety review segment in full before you touch any material, follow the safe order in the order written, stop at once if any stop condition happens, and finish with the disposal steps. Work through the safe order in the safety review, in order, without reordering it. Stop at once if any stop condition happens. Then run the remaining trials and record your own data. No expected value is supplied beforehand and no result is ever filled in for you. If the data is messy, write down what happened and why it may have happened. Finish with the disposal steps in the safety review before anything is packed away.

safety_brief.h3_safety_segment_verbatim:
READ THIS BEFORE YOU TOUCH ANY MATERIAL.
HAZARD (physical): A domestic smoke detector contains a sealed radioactive source and is safe only while it stays intact.
MITIGATION: A smoke detector is never opened, dismantled, or taken apart, and its source is never removed or handled. A working smoke alarm is a safety device and stays installed and intact. This prohibition is not disableable.
HAZARD (physical): Large numbers of small counters spread and can be a choking hazard.
MITIGATION: Work in a shallow tray, keep counters away from young children, and count them back at the end.
HAZARD (emotional): Nuclear topics can raise anxiety about weapons or accidents.
MITIGATION: Content stays on decay physics, energy scale, and engineering trade-offs; the learner may pause or redirect to the materials strand at any point.
SUPERVISION: you may work on this independently. Tell an adult before you start anyway.
SAFE ORDER - do these steps in this order and do not reorder them:
  SAFE ORDER 1. Set the shallow tray down and move young children out of the work area before counters come out.
  SAFE ORDER 2. Count the 100 counters in and record the starting number.
  SAFE ORDER 3. Run each generation, removing and recording before the next throw.
  SAFE ORDER 4. Never open, dismantle, or take apart a smoke detector; it is discussed as a phenomenon and never handled as equipment.
  SAFE ORDER 5. Count every counter back in and confirm the total before leaving.
STOP CONDITIONS - stop at once if any of these happens:
  STOP: Pause if nuclear content becomes distressing and continue with the materials trade-off strand.
  STOP: Stop if anyone begins to open or dismantle a smoke detector.
  STOP: NO RADIOACTIVE SOURCE OF ANY KIND IS USED OR ACQUIRED IN THIS UNIT.
  STOP: Stop for any injury, burn, spill, fume, or allergic reaction and tell the supervising adult.
  STOP: Stop if a material, tool, or step is not the one this lesson specifies.
  STOP: Burn: cool it under running cool water for 20 minutes. Do not use ice, butter, or ointment.
  STOP: Splash in an eye: rinse with running water for 15 minutes, holding the eyelid open, before anything else.
  STOP: Fumes or a strong smell: leave the room, open a window from outside the room, and do not go back in to tidy up.
  STOP: Fire: do not use water. Get everyone out, close the door, and call the emergency number. Smother a very small contained flame with a metal pan lid or a fire blanket only if that is safe to do without reaching over it.
  STOP: If anyone may have swallowed a magnet, a battery, or any material from a lesson, treat it as an emergency and seek medical help at once. Do not wait for symptoms.
  STOP: A pause, break, or switch to the alternative activity is never treated as failure.
DISPOSAL: Counters go back into a labelled container stored out of reach of young children. No radioactive source is used or acquired at any point and no smoke detector is opened, so there is nothing hazardous to dispose of.
ALTERNATIVE (equal credit, no special equipment): Model half-life with a single die and tally marks on paper instead of 100 coins, then complete the trade-off analysis from published materials data. Paper only.
ALWAYS - these rules hold in every lesson and nobody can switch them off:
  ALWAYS: Never mix household cleaning products; bleach combined with ammonia or acid releases toxic gas.
  ALWAYS: Never connect any investigation to mains electricity; low-voltage cells only.
  ALWAYS: Never fully seal a reacting, fermenting, oxidising, or warm mixture in any container.
  ALWAYS: Never have a flammable liquid open in the same room as a flame, hob, pilot light, heater, lamp, charger, or battery.
  ALWAYS: Never use alcohol, or any other fuel, for a flame demonstration; no open-flame demonstration is used anywhere in this package.
  ALWAYS: Never light, strike, or operate an open flame or a hob, burner, or pilot light for any investigation in this package; no lesson requires one.
  ALWAYS: Never cut, tear, puncture, or open a sealed commercial product - cold pack, hand warmer, glow stick, or smoke detector.
  ALWAYS: Never look at the sun directly or through any lens, filter, grating, or camera.
  ALWAYS: Never require a photograph, video, or voice recording as evidence of completion.
  ALWAYS: Never request or record a learner body measurement, health measurement, or medical history.
  ALWAYS: Never present invented measurements as real experimental results.

disqualifying_errors: Claiming fission is the combining of nuclei.
Claiming fission energy comes from breaking chemical bonds.
Claiming a reactor's fuel can undergo a nuclear explosion in the manner of a weapon.
fixed_facts: Fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus into lighter nuclei, releasing energy and typically neutrons.
scientific_correctness_authority.out_of_scope: Reactor engineering, cross sections, and criticality calculations are beyond this course.
relationships: Fission of a heavy nucleus releases energy because the products are more tightly bound per nucleon than the original nucleus.
Released neutrons can induce further fissions, which is the basis of a chain reaction.
Control of a fission reactor works by controlling the number of neutrons available to induce further fission.

disqualifying_errors: Claiming mass is conserved exactly in nuclear reactions in the same way it is in chemical ones.
Claiming chemical and nuclear energy releases are of comparable magnitude per reaction.
Claiming nuclear energy comes from breaking bonds between atoms.
fixed_facts: In nuclear reactions a small amount of mass is converted to energy, following the mass-energy relationship, which is why nuclear energy release is millions of times larger per event than chemical energy release.
scientific_correctness_authority.out_of_scope: Relativistic mechanics and binding energy computation are beyond this course.
relationships: The energy released in a nuclear reaction corresponds to the mass difference between the initial and final nuclei.
Chemical reactions rearrange electrons and involve mass changes far too small to measure; nuclear reactions do not.
This difference in scale is why a small mass of nuclear fuel yields energy comparable to a very large mass of chemical fuel.
